newsitem.title: FRANCE: French president, government powers unevenly split.
newsitem.headline: French president, government powers unevenly split.

text.p: France's constitution splits power unevenly between the president and the government, leaving it uncertain who would have the final say in policy on European Union issues if there were a clash.

A swing to the left in round one of France's parliamentary election on Sunday has raised the possibility that conservative President Jacques Chirac may be forced to share power with a left-wing government after the June 1 runoff.

The 1958 Fifth Republic constitution is vague about who has responsibility for issues where domestic and international policy overlap -- such as preparations for the planned single European currency from 1999 under the Maastricht Treaty.

The president is the guarantor of "respect for treaties". But the constitution also says "the government determines and conducts the nation's policy". Parliament is entrusted with approving the budget presented by the government.

The late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand, forced into "cohabitation" from 1986 to 1988 and 1993 to 1995, carved out a pre-eminent role in foreign affairs under the ill-defined rules. He avoided discord on foreign policy with similarly pro-European centre-right governments.

But opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin's insistence that he would not impose further austerity to meet the strict budget criteria for joining the euro single currency could contain the seeds of a clash.
Jospin has also said he would seek to negotiate four conditions for joining the euro, including participation of Spain and Italy from the start.

It is unclear how far Chirac could invoke his duty to ensure respect for treaties to challenge domestic spending plans that might push the budget deficit above the three percent of gross domestic product set as a criterion for joining the euro.
Jacques Attali, a former adviser to Mitterrand, said that a third bout of cohabitation "could be an extremely ambiguous situation as the rules have not been clarified".

"With the euro, the border between domestic and foreign policy will be different than before. The role of the government, compared with that of the president, will be much more important than before," he said.

Many analysts believe Jospin, if he were prime minister, would not jeopardise a treaty that is one of the Socialists' proudest achievements -- Mitterrand was a major architect. They expect that despite campaign rhetoric he would follow policies little different from the current centre-right coalition.
The constitution says the president promulgates laws. He can demand that parliament re-examine them if he does not like them, but unlike an American president, he has no formal veto right.

The French president is also charged with upholding the constitution, appointing the prime minister and presiding over all cabinet meetings. He is head of the armed forces, although the constitution says the prime minister is "responsible for national defence".

In a crisis, the president can take "measures demanded by circumstances" if the "integrity of (French) territory or the execution of international commitments are threatened in a serious and immediate way and the regular functioning of the public authorities is interrupted".

The president's other major weapon is the power to dissolve the National Assembly and call a snap election, as Chirac did last month. But he would have to wait at least a year from the start of the new legislature before doing so again.
